speaker: Sean Carroll
title: Sean Carroll: General Relativity, Quantum Mechanics, Black Holes & Aliens (#428)
question: In thermodynamics, how does complex life fit into the second law if entropy in an isolated system always increases?
guest: If you start with a system isolated from the rest of the universe at low entropy, there's almost a theorem that very low entropy looks pretty simple, because there's only a small number of ways to rearrange the parts to look like that. There's also almost a theorem that at maximum entropy, the system looks simple because it's all smeared out. So entropy in an isolated system only goes up—that's the second law of thermodynamics—but complexity starts low, goes up, and then goes down again. Sometimes people mistakenly think complexity or life is fighting against the second law of thermodynamics, fighting against the increase of entropy. That is precisely the wrong way to think about it. We are surfers riding the wave of increasing entropy; we rely on increasing entropy to survive. This table maintains its stability mechanically—its molecules have forces on each other and it holds up. You and I aren't like that. We maintain our stability dynamically by ingesting fuel—food, water, and air—burning it, and increasing its entropy. We are out-of-equilibrium quasi-steady-state systems using the fuel the universe gives us in the form of low-entropy energy to maintain our stability.

points.core: Complexity rises then falls back to simplicity as entropy increases monotonically.
points.note: Accept: complexity starts low at very low entropy, peaks at intermediate entropy, and drops again at maximum smeared-out equilibrium entropy while entropy only increases. Do not credit: claiming complexity rises monotonically with entropy or strictly opposes it.

points.core: Living organisms rely on increasing entropy rather than fighting the second law.
points.note: Accept: life rides the wave of increasing entropy or requires entropy growth to survive, refuting the misconception that life fights thermodynamics. Do not credit: claiming life locally violates the second law of thermodynamics.

points.core: Organisms maintain stability dynamically by burning low-entropy fuel to increase total entropy.
points.note: Accept: out-of-equilibrium quasi-steady-state systems ingesting low-entropy energy (food, sunlight, air) and dissipating higher-entropy waste to stay stable. Do not credit: vague mentions of eating food without linking to low-entropy fuel or nonequilibrium stability.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Complex life doesn't violate the second law because living things are not isolated systems. The law says total entropy can't decrease in a system that exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings; an organism, and the Earth's biosphere as a whole, constantly exchanges both.

Life builds and maintains its internal order by taking in low-entropy energy and expelling higher-entropy waste. Earth receives sunlight as a relatively small number of high-energy photons and radiates the same energy back to space as a much larger number of low-energy infrared photons, which carries away far more entropy than arrived. Plants capture part of that flow through photosynthesis, and animals eat that stored chemical order, releasing heat, carbon dioxide and other disordered waste.

So the local decrease in entropy inside a cell or organism is more than paid for by a larger increase in the surroundings. The total entropy of Sun, Earth and space still rises. In fact, living things speed up entropy production overall, as Schrödinger noted when he described organisms as feeding on "negative entropy."

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Living organisms do not violate the second law of thermodynamics because they are open systems, whereas the law requires entropy to increase only in isolated systems that exchange neither energy nor matter with their surroundings. Life builds and maintains intricate internal order, locally keeping its own entropy low, by continuously consuming low-entropy energy and matter—such as sunlight or chemical nutrients—and expelling high-entropy waste and heat into the environment. Because every metabolic and biological process is irreversible and less than completely efficient, the entropy released into the surroundings always exceeds the local reduction of entropy within the organism. Consequently, the combined entropy of the organism and its environment steadily increases, fully satisfying the second law across the broader universe. Far from defying thermodynamics, living things act as dissipative structures that spontaneously self-organize as they channel and degrade concentrated free energy into dispersed heat. Complex life thrives on Earth because our planet is itself an open system, absorbing a steady stream of low-entropy solar photons and radiating high-entropy infrared heat into the cold sink of space.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Living things don't break the second law because they aren't isolated systems. The law says total entropy can't decrease in an isolated system. An organism is an open system that constantly trades energy and matter with its surroundings, so it can lower its own entropy as long as it raises the entropy of its environment by at least as much.

On Earth, the Sun sends us energy as a relatively small number of high-energy visible photons. Earth radiates the same amount of energy back to space as many more low-energy infrared photons, which carry far more entropy. That flow from low to high entropy is what drives life. Plants use sunlight to build ordered molecules like sugars. Animals eat those molecules, keep their own structure intact, and give off heat, CO₂, and waste, all of which add to the disorder around them. Schrödinger described this in 1944 as organisms "feeding on negative entropy."

Prigogine called living systems "dissipative structures": ordered patterns that last only while energy keeps flowing through them, like hurricanes or convection cells. In total, the order life builds is far outweighed by the entropy it exports, so the universe's entropy still goes up.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
The second law of thermodynamics states that total entropy never decreases in an isolated system—one that exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings. Living organisms, and Earth’s biosphere as a whole, are not isolated systems; they are open systems that continuously exchange both matter and energy with their environment.

Complex life builds and maintains its internal order by importing low-entropy energy—primarily sunlight, or chemical energy from food and hydrothermal vents—and using it to drive cellular processes. In doing so, organisms release waste and dissipate low-grade heat back into their surroundings. This exported heat and waste increase the entropy of the environment by more than the local decrease in entropy within the organism.

When you consider the complete system—the living organism together with its environment, or Earth together with the Sun and deep space—total entropy still increases. Far from violating the second law, life is a local pocket of order sustained by a net increase in disorder elsewhere.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The second law says that the total entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease. A living organism is an open system. It takes in energy and matter, uses them to build and repair its structures, and releases heat and waste. The entropy generated by these processes can more than offset any decrease in entropy within the organism.

The same principle applies on a planetary scale. Earth absorbs sunlight and radiates energy back into space as infrared radiation. Because Earth emits at a much lower temperature than the Sun, the outgoing radiation carries more entropy per unit of energy. That energy flow helps sustain complex life while total entropy increases.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra

Complex life is compatible with the second law because an organism is an open system. It exchanges energy and matter with its surroundings. A cell can use energy from sunlight or food to build and maintain organized structures. In doing so, it releases heat and waste into its environment. Any local decrease in entropy is offset by an increase in entropy elsewhere.

The second law applies to the total entropy of an isolated system. That total cannot decrease. It increases during irreversible processes, including metabolism, and stays constant in the ideal reversible limit.
